documents.full_content: Identity and Access Management (IAM) in Google Cloud is the system that controls who can do what on which resources. Rather than assigning permissions individually, IAM uses **roles** which bundle permissions together. There are three types of roles: predefined, custom, and basic roles. IAM follows the principle of least privilege: you grant the smallest set of permissions needed for a user’s job. Access is granted by binding a member to a role at a certain resource level.

documents.title: Service Accounts and Application Identity
documents.content: Service accounts are special accounts used by applications or services to authenticate with Google Cloud APIs. documents.full_content: Service accounts are special accounts used by applications or services to authenticate with Google Cloud APIs. They have their own set of IAM permissions and are a fundamental part of securely calling GCP services from code. A best practice is to use **Workload Identity Federation** or service account impersonation rather than long-lived JSON keys. For on-GCP workloads, one can attach a service account to the compute and it will automatically obtain credentials.

documents.title: Resource Hierarchy and IAM Inheritance
documents.content: Google Cloud organizes resources in a hierarchy for management and IAM inheritance. At the top is the **Organization** node. Under that, you can create **Folders**, and within org/folders are **Projects** – the fundamental unit where resources reside. IAM policies applied at higher levels propagate
documents.full_content: Google Cloud organizes resources in a hierarchy for management and IAM inheritance. At the top is the **Organization** node. Under that, you can create **Folders**, and within org/folders are **Projects** – the fundamental unit where resources reside. IAM policies applied at higher levels propagate down: if you grant a role at the Org level, it applies to all resources in all projects. This hierarchy allows setting broad policies and more granular ones at folder or project level.

documents.title: Cloud Storage Overview
documents.content: Cloud Storage (GCS) is Google Cloud’s unified object storage service, used to store and retrieve files (objects) of any size. It’s durable (11 nines of durability) and highly available, backing use cases from serving website assets to data lakes. GCS organizes data into buckets, which can be regiona
documents.full_content: Cloud Storage (GCS) is Google Cloud’s unified object storage service, used to store and retrieve files (objects) of any size. It’s durable (11 nines of durability) and highly available, backing use cases from serving website assets to data lakes. GCS organizes data into buckets, which can be regional or multi-regional. You can access objects via RESTful API, client libraries, or command-line, and features like object versioning and lifecycle management make it easy to manage data.

documents.title: Cloud Storage Standard Class
documents.content: **Standard storage** is the default storage class in Cloud Storage, optimized for frequent access and low latency. It's best for hot data and supports use cases where data is regularly accessed or updated. Standard storage can be used in single regions, dual-regions, or multi-regions, offering the h
documents.full_content: **Standard storage** is the default storage class in Cloud Storage, optimized for frequent access and low latency. It's best for hot data and supports use cases where data is regularly accessed or updated. Standard storage can be used in single regions, dual-regions, or multi-regions, offering the highest availability for critical workloads. Though it has the highest storage cost, it has no minimum retention period and no extra charges for data retrieval.

documents.title: Cloud Storage Nearline Class
documents.content: **Nearline storage** is a low-cost, highly durable storage class meant for infrequently accessed data (roughly once a month or less). It offers slightly lower availability and imposes a 30-day minimum storage duration and a small per-GB retrieval fee. This makes it suitable for data you access occas
documents.full_content: **Nearline storage** is a low-cost, highly durable storage class meant for infrequently accessed data (roughly once a month or less). It offers slightly lower availability and imposes a 30-day minimum storage duration and a small per-GB retrieval fee. This makes it suitable for data you access occasionally, like monthly analytics data or backups. The trade-off is significantly lower storage cost than Standard.

documents.title: Cloud Storage Coldline Class
documents.content: **Coldline storage** is designed for even less frequently accessed data (on the order of once per quarter). It has a 90-day minimum storage duration and higher data retrieval fees than Nearline, but storage cost per GB is lower. Coldline is ideal for archiving data that still needs quick access when
documents.full_content: **Coldline storage** is designed for even less frequently accessed data (on the order of once per quarter). It has a 90-day minimum storage duration and higher data retrieval fees than Nearline, but storage cost per GB is lower. Coldline is ideal for archiving data that still needs quick access when retrieved. When retrieval does happen, you pay more per GB and per operation, so Coldline is best when reads are very rare.

documents.title: Cloud Storage Archive Class
documents.content: **Archive storage** is the lowest-cost, highly durable storage service for data that is rarely accessed (perhaps once a year or less). Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration and the highest access costs, but data is still available within milliseconds when needed. It's intended for true cold
documents.full_content: **Archive storage** is the lowest-cost, highly durable storage service for data that is rarely accessed (perhaps once a year or less). Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration and the highest access costs, but data is still available within milliseconds when needed. It's intended for true cold archives: data kept mostly for compliance or historical record. Archive storage trades off some availability and incurs significant retrieval cost.

documents.title: Cloud Storage Autoclass
documents.content: Autoclass is a feature of Cloud Storage that automatically manages storage class transitions for objects within a bucket. When enabled, Autoclass will monitor the access patterns of objects and transparently transition them to the most cost-effective storage class over time. For instance, an object
documents.full_content: Autoclass is a feature of Cloud Storage that automatically manages storage class transitions for objects within a bucket. When enabled, Autoclass will monitor the access patterns of objects and transparently transition them to the most cost-effective storage class over time. For instance, an object in Standard class may be automatically moved to Nearline, Coldline, or Archive if it goes unaccessed. Autoclass removes the guesswork of choosing a storage class upfront.

documents.title: Cloud Pub/Sub Overview
documents.content: Cloud Pub/Sub is a global, fully-managed messaging service that allows decoupling of producers and consumers in distributed systems. It follows a publish/subscribe model: producers send messages to topics, and subscribers receive those messages asynchronously. Pub/Sub is designed for high throughput
documents.full_content: Cloud Pub/Sub is a global, fully-managed messaging service that allows decoupling of producers and consumers in distributed systems. It follows a publish/subscribe model: producers send messages to topics, and subscribers receive those messages asynchronously. Pub/Sub is designed for high throughput and reliability; it durably stores messages until delivered and can automatically scale to millions of messages per second. Common use cases include event ingestion, decoupling microservices, and feeding streaming data into systems like Dataflow.

documents.title: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics
documents.content: Cloud Pub/Sub provides **at-least-once** delivery of messages to subscribers, meaning a message will be delivered at least once but possibly multiple times. This can occur if a subscriber doesn’t acknowledge a message before the deadline or if a transient failure triggers a retry. Therefore, subscri
documents.full_content: Cloud Pub/Sub provides **at-least-once** delivery of messages to subscribers, meaning a message will be delivered at least once but possibly multiple times. This can occur if a subscriber doesn’t acknowledge a message before the deadline or if a transient failure triggers a retry. Therefore, subscribers should be designed to handle duplicate messages (e.g., by using message IDs for de-duplication or making operations idempotent). Pub/Sub also supports **ordering keys** to guarantee ordered delivery of messages with the same key.

documents.title: Pub/Sub Push vs Pull Subscriptions
documents.content: Pub/Sub offers two types of subscription delivery: **pull** (the subscriber client explicitly requests messages) and **push** (Pub/Sub sends messages to an HTTPS endpoint). In pull mode, subscribers have more control. In push mode, Pub/Sub acts like a webhook sender; the service must respond with a
documents.full_content: Pub/Sub offers two types of subscription delivery: **pull** (the subscriber client explicitly requests messages) and **push** (Pub/Sub sends messages to an HTTPS endpoint). In pull mode, subscribers have more control. In push mode, Pub/Sub acts like a webhook sender; the service must respond with a success code to ACK. Push can simplify event-driven architectures, but requires a resilient endpoint. In either mode, if a message isn’t acknowledged within the ack deadline, Pub/Sub will redeliver it.

documents.title: Pub/Sub Dead Letter Topics
documents.content: To handle messages that cannot be processed successfully, Pub/Sub supports dead letter topics. You can configure a subscription with a dead letter topic and a maximum delivery attempt count. If a message is not acknowledged too many times, Pub/Sub will route it to the dead letter topic instead of re
documents.full_content: To handle messages that cannot be processed successfully, Pub/Sub supports dead letter topics. You can configure a subscription with a dead letter topic and a maximum delivery attempt count. If a message is not acknowledged too many times, Pub/Sub will route it to the dead letter topic instead of retrying further. This prevents endlessly reprocessing 'poison pill' messages that consistently fail and allows separate handling of those messages. Using dead letters improves system resilience.

documents.title: Cloud Composer (Managed Airflow)
documents.content: Cloud Composer is a managed workflow orchestration service built on Apache Airflow, allowing you to create, schedule, and monitor complex workflows on Google Cloud. You define DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs of tasks) in Python, and Cloud Composer runs them on a managed Kubernetes cluster in GCP. This
documents.full_content: Cloud Composer is a managed workflow orchestration service built on Apache Airflow, allowing you to create, schedule, and monitor complex workflows on Google Cloud. You define DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs of tasks) in Python, and Cloud Composer runs them on a managed Kubernetes cluster in GCP. This means you get all of Airflow’s features without managing its infrastructure. Typical use cases include orchestrating data pipelines. Cloud Composer 2 introduced an autoscaling environment with better isolation.

documents.title: Cloud Run (Serverless Containers)
documents.content: Cloud Run is a fully-managed, serverless platform for running containerized applications without managing servers. It takes any container image and runs it as a stateless service that automatically scales up from zero to handle incoming requests and scales back down to zero when idle (pay-per-use mo
documents.full_content: Cloud Run is a fully-managed, serverless platform for running containerized applications without managing servers. It takes any container image and runs it as a stateless service that automatically scales up from zero to handle incoming requests and scales back down to zero when idle (pay-per-use model). Cloud Run services are typically invoked via HTTP requests, and each instance can handle a configurable number of concurrent requests. Its simplicity and support for any language make it a popular choice for deploying microservices.

documents.title: Cloud Run vs Cloud Functions
documents.content: Both Cloud Run and Cloud Functions are serverless compute offerings. **Cloud Functions** is a Functions-as-a-Service platform where you deploy small pieces of code that execute in response to events. It’s language-runtime limited and suited for lightweight, standalone tasks. **Cloud Run**, in contra
documents.full_content: Both Cloud Run and Cloud Functions are serverless compute offerings. **Cloud Functions** is a Functions-as-a-Service platform where you deploy small pieces of code that execute in response to events. It’s language-runtime limited and suited for lightweight, standalone tasks. **Cloud Run**, in contrast, runs arbitrary container images, allowing you to bring your own runtime and dependencies. Cloud Run is suited for building microservices or handling workloads that don’t fit in the function model. Cloud Functions auto-scales instances per function invocation, whereas Cloud Run allows concurrency.

documents.title: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
documents.content: GKE is Google Cloud’s managed Kubernetes service, which simplifies deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications using Kubernetes. GKE provides two modes: **Standard**, where you manage the node VMs; and **Autopilot**, where Google also manages the node infrastructure and auto-provisio
documents.full_content: GKE is Google Cloud’s managed Kubernetes service, which simplifies deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications using Kubernetes. GKE provides two modes: **Standard**, where you manage the node VMs; and **Autopilot**, where Google also manages the node infrastructure and auto-provisions resources. In Autopilot, you only pay for pod resources used. GKE integrates with the rest of GCP and offers features like node pools, horizontal and vertical pod auto-scaling, and release channels. It’s often used to orchestrate microservices at scale.

documents.title: Federated Learning for Privacy
documents.content: Federated learning is an approach to model training that keeps user data on devices and only aggregates learned model updates, thereby enhancing privacy. Instead of centralizing all raw data on a server, a federated system sends the current model to user devices, trains on local data, and then sends
documents.full_content: Federated learning is an approach to model training that keeps user data on devices and only aggregates learned model updates, thereby enhancing privacy. Instead of centralizing all raw data on a server, a federated system sends the current model to user devices, trains on local data, and then sends back only model weight updates. No raw personal data leaves the device, mitigating privacy concerns. This technique is used in scenarios like mobile keyboard suggestions or health applications.

documents.title: Differential Privacy
documents.content: Differential privacy is a formal framework for quantifying and limiting the privacy risks in statistical data analysis. A mechanism is differentially private if the inclusion or exclusion of a single individual’s data in a dataset produces only negligible changes in the output of an analysis. Practi
documents.full_content: Differential privacy is a formal framework for quantifying and limiting the privacy risks in statistical data analysis. A mechanism is differentially private if the inclusion or exclusion of a single individual’s data in a dataset produces only negligible changes in the output of an analysis. Practically, this is achieved by adding carefully calibrated random noise to query results or model computations. The strength of privacy protection is controlled by a parameter epsilon (ε) – lower ε means more noise and stronger privacy.

documents.title: Stakeholder Communication in AI Projects
documents.content: Effective communication with stakeholders is critical in AI and cloud projects. Key practices include **clarity and transparency** – explaining technical concepts in plain language and setting realistic expectations. Regular updates help prevent surprises and build trust. It’s also important to tail
documents.full_content: Effective communication with stakeholders is critical in AI and cloud projects. Key practices include **clarity and transparency** – explaining technical concepts in plain language and setting realistic expectations. Regular updates help prevent surprises and build trust. It’s also important to tailor the content to the audience’s interests (e.g., focusing on business impact for an executive versus technical details for an IT lead). Listening and soliciting feedback is part of good communication, as stakeholders often have concerns that need to be addressed.

documents.title: Handling Ambiguity in Requirements
documents.content: AI projects often start with ambiguous or evolving requirements. A key skill is **navigating ambiguity**: instead of being paralyzed by unclear instructions, effective engineers actively seek clarification and iterate towards definition. This can involve asking pointed questions to stakeholders, pro
documents.full_content: AI projects often start with ambiguous or evolving requirements. A key skill is **navigating ambiguity**: instead of being paralyzed by unclear instructions, effective engineers actively seek clarification and iterate towards definition. This can involve asking pointed questions to stakeholders, proposing strawman solutions to elicit reactions, or breaking down a vague goal into smaller experiments. Embracing agile methodologies helps: you might develop a quick proof-of-concept to clarify feasibility and refine requirements as you get feedback.

documents.title: Discussing Trade-offs with Stakeholders
documents.content: In system design, engineers often face trade-offs (accuracy vs latency, cost vs performance, etc.). Communicating these trade-offs to stakeholders is crucial for informed decision-making. This involves clearly explaining each option’s pros and cons in terms that matter to the stakeholder. It’s helpf
documents.full_content: In system design, engineers often face trade-offs (accuracy vs latency, cost vs performance, etc.). Communicating these trade-offs to stakeholders is crucial for informed decision-making. This involves clearly explaining each option’s pros and cons in terms that matter to the stakeholder. It’s helpful to use data or prototypes to back these points. By framing choices in business or user impact terms, you enable stakeholders to weigh what aligns best with their priorities. Documentation of trade-off discussions ensures everyone remembers why a choice was made.

documents.title: Model Extraction Attacks
documents.content: Model extraction (attackers stealing a model) is a technique where an adversary attempts to reconstruct your model by observing its outputs. For instance, by querying a hosted ML model API extensively and analyzing responses, an attacker can train their own model to approximate yours. This can expos
documents.full_content: Model extraction (attackers stealing a model) is a technique where an adversary attempts to reconstruct your model by observing its outputs. For instance, by querying a hosted ML model API extensively and analyzing responses, an attacker can train their own model to approximate yours. This can expose proprietary intellectual property. To mitigate model extraction, one approach is to limit the rate or volume of queries from any one client and monitor for suspicious patterns. Some services intentionally add slight noise to outputs.

documents.title: Training Data Poisoning
documents.content: Training data poisoning is an attack where an adversary injects malicious or misleading data into your model’s training set in order to subtly influence model behavior. For example, if someone can contribute to your dataset, they might label some items incorrectly or insert specially crafted example
documents.full_content: Training data poisoning is an attack where an adversary injects malicious or misleading data into your model’s training set in order to subtly influence model behavior. For example, if someone can contribute to your dataset, they might label some items incorrectly or insert specially crafted examples so that the trained model learns an incorrect mapping or a hidden backdoor trigger. Defenses include securing the data pipeline and using robust training methods that are less sensitive to outliers.

documents.title: AI Bias and Fairness
documents.content: AI models can inadvertently reflect or amplify societal biases present in their training data, leading to potentially unfair or discriminatory outcomes. Ensuring fairness in AI involves steps throughout the model development lifecycle: data curation, bias measurement, and mitigation techniques when
documents.full_content: AI models can inadvertently reflect or amplify societal biases present in their training data, leading to potentially unfair or discriminatory outcomes. Ensuring fairness in AI involves steps throughout the model development lifecycle: data curation, bias measurement, and mitigation techniques when disparities are found. Documentation like **model cards** helps transparency. Bias mitigation might involve rebalancing training data, adding fairness constraints to the model’s optimization, or post-processing outputs.

documents.title: Multi-Region Deployment and Tradeoffs
documents.content: Deploying applications in multiple regions can improve reliability and reduce latency for global users, but it introduces design trade-offs. In an **active-active** multi-region setup, your service runs in two or more regions and serves traffic from all of them. This yields high availability but req
documents.full_content: Deploying applications in multiple regions can improve reliability and reduce latency for global users, but it introduces design trade-offs. In an **active-active** multi-region setup, your service runs in two or more regions and serves traffic from all of them. This yields high availability but requires dealing with data consistency across regions. Alternatively, an **active-passive** (primary/DR) setup is simpler: one region serves until a failover is needed. It’s easier to maintain consistency, but there is downtime in a failover.

documents.title: Batch vs Streaming Data Pipelines
documents.content: Data processing pipelines generally come in two flavors: batch (processing data in large chunks at intervals) and streaming (processing data continuously in real-time). **Batch pipelines** are simpler to implement when real-time results aren’t needed; they can efficiently process large volumes but i
documents.full_content: Data processing pipelines generally come in two flavors: batch (processing data in large chunks at intervals) and streaming (processing data continuously in real-time). **Batch pipelines** are simpler to implement when real-time results aren’t needed; they can efficiently process large volumes but introduce inherent latency. **Streaming pipelines** process data as it arrives, enabling near real-time analytics. The trade-offs: streaming systems are more complex and typically cost more to run continuously.

documents.title: Monolithic vs Microservice Architecture
documents.content: In software architecture, a **monolith** is a single unified application that encompasses all functionalities, whereas a **microservices** architecture splits a system into many small, independent services communicating via APIs. A monolith is simpler to develop initially, but as it grows, it can be
documents.full_content: In software architecture, a **monolith** is a single unified application that encompasses all functionalities, whereas a **microservices** architecture splits a system into many small, independent services communicating via APIs. A monolith is simpler to develop initially, but as it grows, it can become unwieldy. Microservices isolate functionality, allowing each service to be scaled and deployed independently. The trade-off is complexity in orchestration and operations.

documents.title: Cloud Cost Optimization Techniques
documents.content: Optimizing costs in the cloud is about matching resource usage to actual needs and leveraging pricing models. Key strategies on GCP include: **Autoscaling** wherever possible, using **preemptible VMs (Spot VMs)** for fault-tolerant workloads, taking advantage of **sustained use discounts and committ
documents.full_content: Optimizing costs in the cloud is about matching resource usage to actual needs and leveraging pricing models. Key strategies on GCP include: **Autoscaling** wherever possible, using **preemptible VMs (Spot VMs)** for fault-tolerant workloads, taking advantage of **sustained use discounts and committed use discounts** for steady-state workloads, optimizing storage costs by choosing the right storage class and lifecycle rules, and rightsizing your resources using Cloud Monitoring and the Recommender.

documents.title: AutoML vs Custom Model Development
documents.content: AutoML (e.g., Vertex AI AutoML) is ideal for rapid prototyping and baseline models; it handles feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning and model selection automatically. Custom model development allows full control over architecture, optimisation and domain‑specific features, at the cost of more
documents.full_content: AutoML (e.g., Vertex AI AutoML) is ideal for rapid prototyping and baseline models; it handles feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning and model selection automatically. Custom model development allows full control over architecture, optimisation and domain‑specific features, at the cost of more engineering effort. Choose AutoML for time‑constrained prototypes or when machine‑learning expertise is limited, and custom models for production‑critical systems.

documents.title: Model Versioning & Reproducibility
documents.content: Adopt version control for code (Git) and data (DVC or BigQuery snapshots). Track experiments with Vertex AI Experiments or MLflow, and containerise environments with Docker. Use configuration files or parameter stores for pipeline reproducibility, and orchestrate workflows via Kubeflow Pipelines or
documents.full_content: Adopt version control for code (Git) and data (DVC or BigQuery snapshots). Track experiments with Vertex AI Experiments or MLflow, and containerise environments with Docker. Use configuration files or parameter stores for pipeline reproducibility, and orchestrate workflows via Kubeflow Pipelines or Cloud Composer. Maintain thorough documentation of datasets, model parameters and environment dependencies.

documents.title: AI Chatbot Architecture & Key Components
documents.content: A robust chatbot architecture includes a user interface, a conversation flow manager to orchestrate interactions, a language model for NLU and NLG, a context store for conversation history and retrieved knowledge, and integration with external systems (APIs and databases). For production, incorporat
documents.full_content: A robust chatbot architecture includes a user interface, a conversation flow manager to orchestrate interactions, a language model for NLU and NLG, a context store for conversation history and retrieved knowledge, and integration with external systems (APIs and databases). For production, incorporate an API gateway or traffic server to handle scaling, plus network segmentation and encryption to protect data.

documents.title: Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) for Chatbots
documents.content: RAG combines an LLM with a retrieval pipeline. When a user asks a complex question, the system retrieves domain‑specific documents from a knowledge base or FAQ repository and feeds them into the model. This approach grounds responses in factual data, improving relevance and accuracy.
documents.full_content: RAG combines an LLM with a retrieval pipeline. documents.title: Security Best Practices for Chatbots
documents.content: Secure chatbots by minimising PII retention, encrypting sensitive fields with strong keys, and enforcing authentication and authorisation controls on all endpoints. Use network segmentation to isolate critical services, implement continuous monitoring and logging for anomaly detection, and secure we
documents.full_content: Secure chatbots by minimising PII retention, encrypting sensitive fields with strong keys, and enforcing authentication and authorisation controls on all endpoints. Use network segmentation to isolate critical services, implement continuous monitoring and logging for anomaly detection, and secure webhook endpoints.

documents.title: Chatbot Development Best Practices & User Satisfaction
documents.content: Identify your target audience and prioritise high‑impact use cases before building a chatbot. Define success metrics and select vendors based on language support, integration ease and pricing. Make the chatbot accessible, measure user satisfaction via task success rate, latency and retention, and co
documents.full_content: Identify your target audience and prioritise high‑impact use cases before building a chatbot. Define success metrics and select vendors based on language support, integration ease and pricing. Make the chatbot accessible, measure user satisfaction via task success rate, latency and retention, and continuously monitor logs for friction points. A/B testing combined with continuous integration helps refine the bot over time.

documents.title: Guardrails & Safety for Enterprise Agents

documents.full_content: Apply layered controls: (1) **Input sanitization** (PII masking), (2) **Retrieval constraints** (doc ACL filters), (3) **Prompt rules** (citation-required, style forbid), (4) **Model safety settings**, (5) **Output validators** (JSON schema), (6) **Human-in-the-loop** for high-risk actions, (7) **Rate-limiting** + quotas. documents.full_content: Set an SLO (e.g., p95 ≤ 1.5s). Budget: API Gateway (20ms), auth (10ms), retrieval (150–300ms), model call (400–900ms), post-processing (100ms). documents.title: Citations and Grounding Strategy
documents.content: Force every answer to include citations to retrieved passages (URL/document ID). Use chunk IDs with sentence ranges. If retrieval confidence < threshold, the agent asks a clarifying question or returns a safe fallback. Persist citations and decision traces for audits.

Coordinate via shared memory (Redis/AlloyDB)

documents.full_content: **Cloud Run**: serverless, autoscales to zero, effortless ops; great for APIs/agents with spiky demand. **GKE**: pick when you need GPU scheduling, sidecars, sticky memory/state, custom networking, or very high sustained throughput with tight resource control. Many teams start on Run → later move heavy components to GKE.

documents.title: Access Control & Data Isolation
documents.content: Scope service accounts per microservice; least-privilege IAM roles; resource-level conditions. For sensitive data, enable **VPC-SC** perimeter, private ingress, and **CMEK** for storage. Pass user entitlements as filters during retrieval so the model only sees allowed chunks.

documents.title: Evaluating a GenAI System (Beyond BLEU/Rouge)
documents.content: Track **task success**, answer **correctness** (human graded or weak labels), **latency**, **grounding rate**, **deflection** (bot → human), **safety violations**, and **cost per 1k queries**. Run evaluation suites: adversarial prompts, long-context, and OOD queries. Ship dashboards and weekly eval

documents.title: Cost Controls for LLM Workloads
documents.content: Set budgets + alerts. Tune tokens (truncate/summary), use smaller models + rerankers, cache answers. Batch embeddings. Prefer BigQuery for heavy joins. Use **committed use discounts** for steady compute; **Spot VMs** only for batch/offline. Add per-tenant quotas in the API.

documents.title: Disaster Recovery & HA for Agent Systems
documents.content: Multi-zone deployment (Run/GKE), regional storage (GCS/BQ), replayable events (Pub/Sub), and idempotent handlers. Keep stateless services stateless; snapshot indexes and persist doc-to-chunk maps for rebuilds. Test failovers; publish RTO/RPO; include API circuit breakers and backoff.

documents.content: Data classification, retention, and residency; PII minimization; encryption in transit/at rest with **CMEK**; egress restrictions; prompt/response logging (pseudonymized); model and tool allowlists; pen-testing; incident response; red-team plans; vendor DPAs.

documents.title: Observability for Agents
documents.content: Emit structured logs with **trace IDs** across retrieval/model/tool steps. Metrics: p50/p95 latency per step, timeouts, tool error rate, token volume, grounding %, safety blocks. Traces reveal slow retrieval vs slow model. Add alerting on anomalies and budget burn.

documents.title: LLM Choice Strategy
documents.content: Pick by **task** and **SLO**: use a small/fast model for classification/routing; a larger model for synthesis. Consider **context length**, tool-use quality, cost, and eval scores on your datasets. Keep a model-selector abstraction so you can swap models without app rewrites.

documents.title: Hybrid Retrieval (Semantic + Keyword) and Rerank
documents.content: Combine ANN semantic search with keyword/phrase match (BM25) for precision on entities/codes. Use a lightweight **cross-encoder reranker** on the top-k to improve relevance; cap k to keep latency acceptable. In practice this improved factual grounding and reduced hallucinations.

documents.title: Chunking Strategy for Documents
documents.content: Aim for ~200–500 tokens per chunk; keep **semantic boundaries** (headings/paragraphs), add **overlap** (10–20%) for continuity, and store **hierarchy** (doc → section → chunk). Include metadata (source, ACL, updated_at). Re-chunk when schema or model changes.

documents.title: BigQuery SQL: Top-N per Group Pattern
documents.content: Use **ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY metric DESC)** to rank within groups, then **QUALIFY row_number = 1** (or ≤ N). This is better than subqueries for readability/perf and is a standard interview pattern.
documents.full_content: Use **ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY metric DESC)** to rank within groups, then **QUALIFY row_number = 1** (or ≤ N). This is better than subqueries for readability/perf and is a standard interview pattern.

documents.title: Preventing Prompt Injection
documents.content: Never pass raw retrieved text as instructions. Put tool specs and policies in **system** instructions only. Constrain tools (schemas/allowlists), sanitize HTML/URLs, and perform **content scanning** on retrieved context. Treat model outputs as untrusted until validated.
documents.full_content: Never pass raw retrieved text as instructions. Put tool specs and policies in **system** instructions only. Constrain tools (schemas/allowlists), sanitize HTML/URLs, and perform **content scanning** on retrieved context. Treat model outputs as untrusted until validated.

documents.title: Evaluating RAG vs Fine-Tuning
documents.content: **RAG**: best when knowledge changes often or is proprietary; cheap to update. **Fine-tuning**: good for style, domain lingo, or structured outputs when RAG is insufficient. Often use both: RAG for facts + lightweight fine-tune or adapters for format/voice.

documents.title: Caching Layers That Matter
documents.content: 1) **Embedding cache** by text hash. 2) **Retrieval cache** (query→doc IDs) for hot queries. 3) **Answer cache** with TTL and user-/tenant-scoped keys. 4) **Tool results cache**. Invalidate on doc update or schema change.

documents.title: Cloud Run Autoscaling Controls
documents.content: Use **min/max instances**, concurrency, and CPU always-on for low cold-start latency. For bursty traffic, allow higher concurrency if your handler is non-blocking. Set per-revision configs and canary with **traffic splitting**.
documents.full_content: Use **min/max instances**, concurrency, and CPU always-on for low cold-start latency. For bursty traffic, allow higher concurrency if your handler is non-blocking. Set per-revision configs and canary with **traffic splitting**.

documents.title: Pipelines for Embeddings at Scale
documents.content: Batch via Dataflow or parallel Cloud Run jobs. Use backpressure and dead-letter queues (Pub/Sub). Persist progress checkpoints and retry on rate-limit. Monitor TPS and token spend; scale workers horizontally with a max concurrency per model endpoint.

documents.title: Vector Index Hygiene
documents.content: Maintain index versions; record embedding model/version; snapshot indexes; rebuild on drift/model change. Track recall@k on a labeled set; watch for index saturation. Keep warm replicas for failover.
documents.full_content: Maintain index versions; record embedding model/version; snapshot indexes; rebuild on drift/model change. Track recall@k on a labeled set; watch for index saturation. Keep warm replicas for failover.

documents.title: AlloyDB with pgvector vs Managed Vector Store
documents.content: AlloyDB pgvector gives SQL + transactional semantics with vectors (great for app state + search in one DB). Managed vector (Vertex AI Vector Search) wins on **ultra-low latency** and index scaling. I use AlloyDB for hybrid transactional/semantic needs and Vector Search for the RAG hot path.

documents.title: Role-Based & Attribute-Based Access for RAG
documents.content: Store ACLs at doc/section. At query time, apply **ABAC filters** (tenant, department, clearance). Emit authorization decisions in logs. This prevents leakage when the LLM tries to combine chunks from different tenants.

documents.title: Handling Long Context
documents.content: Stick to short, curated contexts. Summarize chains (map-reduce). Use retrieval-augmented **memory** for dialog state (structured slots rather than replaying long transcripts). If you must go long, use models with long-context windows and add rerankers.

documents.title: Canarying and A/B Testing with LLMs
documents.content: Ship new prompts/models to a small traffic slice. Track deltas on accuracy, latency, and cost. Roll back on degradation. Maintain side-by-side dashboards. Periodically re-baseline old variants because data drift is real.

documents.title: Backpressure & Timeouts in Orchestrations
documents.content: Set stage-level timeouts and circuit breakers. Use bounded queues and async tool calls. If a tool stalls, return best-effort answer with available citations. This keeps p95/p99 within SLO and avoids request pile-ups.
documents.full_content: Set stage-level timeouts and circuit breakers. Use bounded queues and async tool calls. If a tool stalls, return best-effort answer with available citations. This keeps p95/p99 within SLO and avoids request pile-ups.

documents.title: Data Residency & Regional Design
documents.content: Pick a primary region close to users/data. Keep all stateful services and storage in-region. Replicate read-only copies to secondary for DR. Enforce egress limits; document residency in your data processing agreement.
documents.full_content: Pick a primary region close to users/data. Keep all stateful services and storage in-region. Replicate read-only copies to secondary for DR. Enforce egress limits; document residency in your data processing agreement.

documents.title: PII Handling in Logs and Indexes
documents.content: Hash or tokenize identifiers; drop free-text PII at ingestion where possible; implement **subject access** and delete flows. For logs, keep only what’s essential. Tie retention to compliance rules.

documents.content: Write runbooks for: safety violation spikes, latency spikes, tool outage, index corruption, cost overrun. Include rollback steps, traffic shifting, cache warmup, and communications. Run game-days quarterly.

documents.title: Your SQL Walkthrough (BigQuery) — Window + QUALIFY
documents.content: Explain how you’d de-duplicate customer events by (user_id, day): use **ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY user_id, DATE(event_ts) ORDER BY event_ts DESC)** and **QUALIFY row_number = 1** to keep the latest per user/day; mention partitioned tables and clustering for cost/latency.

documents.title: Tool execution security
documents.content: Sandbox tools; limit outbound network; scrub inputs; enforce timeouts and quotas per user; log arguments; require explicit user consent for risky tools.

documents.title: Schema-structured outputs
documents.content: Constrain model outputs to JSON schema and validate. On failure, request repair. This enables reliable downstream automation.

documents.title: Knowledge freshness policy
documents.content: Define TTLs for retrieved content; date-stamp answers; prefer newest sources; annotate stale knowledge to avoid hallucinated ‘recent’ facts.

documents.title: A/B testing prompt variants
documents.content: Experiment with few-shot vs zero-shot, retrieval depth, and temperature. Track task success and guardrail violation rates; roll forward only if improvements are significant.

documents.title: BigQuery performance gotchas
documents.content: Avoid SELECT * on huge tables; use partition filters; pre-aggregate large joins; consider approximate functions (APPROX_*).

documents.title: Event-driven agent workflows
documents.content: Pub/Sub triggers for async steps (indexing, notifications); store status in a DB; retries with DLQ for flaky partners.
documents.full_content: Pub/Sub triggers for async steps (indexing, notifications); store status in a DB; retries with DLQ for flaky partners.

documents.title: Access control for internal assistants
documents.content: Propagate user identity (OIDC/JWT) and check ACLs before retrieval; filter docs by user entitlements; log denials.
documents.full_content: Propagate user identity (OIDC/JWT) and check ACLs before retrieval; filter docs by user entitlements; log denials.

documents.title: Index-build pipelines
documents.content: Use Dataflow for parsing, chunking, embedding, and writing vectors. Trigger incremental updates on file changes and schedule periodic re-embeds.
documents.full_content: Use Dataflow for parsing, chunking, embedding, and writing vectors. Trigger incremental updates on file changes and schedule periodic re-embeds.

documents.title: Rate limits & abuse prevention
documents.content: Throttle by API key/IP/user; require reCAPTCHA for public endpoints; track suspicious patterns and blocklists.
documents.full_content: Throttle by API key/IP/user; require reCAPTCHA for public endpoints; track suspicious patterns and blocklists.

documents.title: Post-incident reviews for LLM outages
documents.content: Run blameless PMs; classify causes (provider, prompt, retrieval, tool). Add tests and alerts to prevent repeats.
documents.full_content: Run blameless PMs; classify causes (provider, prompt, retrieval, tool). Add tests and alerts to prevent repeats.

documents.title: SQL: slowly changing dimensions (SCD) and change tracking
documents.content: Use effective_from/effective_to with windowing to derive current vs history; dedupe overlapping ranges; rely on QUALIFY to pick current rows.

documents.title: GPU vs CPU for embeddings and inference
documents.content: Use GPUs for high-throughput embedding/inference; CPUs are fine for low-QPS and background indexing. Consider model-hosted options to avoid infra.

documents.content: Balance chunk size with overlap to preserve context without ballooning index size; evaluate where answers come from to tune.

documents.content: Strip boilerplate, normalize headings, and preserve semantic sections; store source URIs for citations.

documents.content: Run DR drills quarterly; automate failover; verify data integrity and index consistency post-recovery.

documents.content: Use Secret Manager; rotate keys; never bake secrets into images; enforce least privilege service accounts.

documents.content: Document data flows; classification and retention policies; ensure third-party tools meet org standards and sign DPAs.

documents.content: Support keyboard navigation and screen readers; provide short/long answer modes; handle multilingual users gracefully.
